The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

If $X$ has Lebesgue density $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and $\int f\ln f$ is a finite real number, its differential entropy in nats is $h(X):=-\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x)\ln f(x)\,dx$. If $(X,S)$ has conditional densities $f_{X|S=s}$ for almost every $s$ and the indicated integral is finite, set $h(X|S):=\int h(f_{X|S=s})\,dP_S(s)$. We use only these finite-integral cases; differential entropy is not defined here by a formal subtraction of possibly infinite quantities.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If a random vector $X\in\mathbb R^d$ has a Lebesgue density, finite mean $m$, positive-definite covariance $K$, and finite differential entropy $h(X)=-\int f\ln f$, then
$$h(X)\le \frac12\ln\bigl((2\pi e)^d\det K\bigr).$$
Equality holds exactly when $X$ has the Gaussian law $N_d(m,K)$.

Assume AC. Let $Z\in\mathbb C$ have a Lebesgue density, finite mean $\mu$, finite differential entropy, and positive-definite real covariance matrix $K$ for $(\operatorname{Re}Z,\operatorname{Im}Z)$. Put $\sigma^2=\mathbb E|Z-\mu|^2=\operatorname{tr}K$. Then
$$h(Z)\le\ln(\pi e\sigma^2).$$
Equality holds exactly for the circular complex Gaussian law $\mathcal{CN}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with density $(\pi\sigma^2)^{-1}\exp(-|z-\mu|^2/\sigma^2)$.

Let $f$ be a Lebesgue probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ with $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$ and $\int |x|^2f(x)\,dx<\infty$. Then $\int f(x)|\ln f(x)|\,dx<\infty$, so the differential entropy in [[def-it-real-differential-entropy]] is a finite real number.

derivations.claim: The output density is the convolution $f_Y(y)=\int g_Z(y-ax)P_X(dx)$, so $0<f_Y\le\|g_Z\|_\infty<\infty$, and $Y$ has finite second moment. By [F5], $\int f_Y|\ln f_Y|<\infty$, so [F2] defines a finite differential entropy $h(Y)$.

The positive Gaussian noise density makes $f_Y(y)>0$. Relative to $P_X(dx)f_Y(y)dy$, the joint law of $(X,Y)$ has density $g_Z(y-ax)/f_Y(y)$. By [F1], $$I(X;Y)=\int P_X(dx)\int g_Z(y-ax)\ln\frac{g_Z(y-ax)}{f_Y(y)}dy=h(Y)-h(Z).$$ The two logarithmic integrals are finite by step 1.1 and the Gaussian density formula, so this identity involves no subtraction of infinite quantities.

Independence gives $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=1+|a|^2v$. Apply [F3] and the real Gaussian noise entropy in the real case, or [F4] and $h(Z)=\ln(\pi e)$ in the complex case. Step 2.1 then yields $I(X;Y)\le\kappa\ln(1+|a|^2v)$ nats. Since $v\le\mathbb E|X|^2$, division by $\ln2$ gives the corresponding bit bound. For the stated Gaussian inputs, the output is Gaussian of the same real or circular complex type and attains the matching maximum-entropy equality.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

Assume AC. Let $Z\in\mathbb C$ have a Lebesgue density, finite mean $\mu$, finite differential entropy, and positive-definite real covariance matrix $K$ for $(\operatorname{Re}Z,\operatorname{Im}Z)$. Put $\sigma^2=\mathbb E|Z-\mu|^2=\operatorname{tr}K$. Then

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

derivations.claim: If $(T,S)$ are Gaussian-smoothed finite-second-moment variables, then $h(T|S)=h(T-kS|S)\le h(T-kS)\le\log_2(\pi e\operatorname{Var}(T-kS))$ for every complex $k$. The first identity is conditional translation and the first inequality is conditional mutual-information nonnegativity; the second is [F2]. A finite-dimensional convolution with a nonsingular Gaussian has a density bounded by the peak of that Gaussian and finite second moment; [F3], applied after identifying complex vectors with real vectors, therefore makes every relevant joint, marginal, and residual differential entropy finite. In particular the pairs $(Y_1^n,S_1^n)$ and $(Y_2^n,S_2^n)$ have nonsingular independent receiver-noise coordinates, and the degraded pair below has nonsingular joint Gaussian noise when $s>t$. Their conditional entropies are differences of these finite joint and marginal entropies. For conditioning additionally on $X_1^n$, which need not have a density, first subtract its known translated contribution; independence removes that conditioning and leaves the nonsingular smoothed pair $(h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n,S_2^n)$. For a channel with conditional density $w(t|x)$ and positive output density $f_T(t)$, the joint-to-product density ratio is $w(t|x)/f_T(t)$. Thus [F5] gives $I(X;T)=\int\ln(w(t|x)/f_T(t))\,dP_{X,T}$. When $T=BX+Z$ with independent nonsingular Gaussian $Z$, the two log integrals are finite by [F3] and the quadratic Gaussian log density, and this integral equals $h(T)-h(Z)$. The same calculation with conditional densities justifies the conditional entropy identities used below, since their joint and marginal entropies are finite as established above. At zero signal power the same Gaussian density argument applies without alteration. Coordinate entropy chain rules give $h(T^n|S^n)\le\sum_j h(T_j|S_j)$.

Suppose $s>t$ and set $U^n=\sqrt{s}X^n+Z^n$, $V^n=\sqrt{t/s}\,U^n+\sqrt{1-t/s}\,W^n$. The marginal law of $V^n$ is the lower-SNR channel and $X^n-U^n-V^n$ is Markov. Thus the difference of the two output entropies equals $I(X^n;U^n|V^n)=h(U^n|V^n)-n\log_2(\pi e[1-t/s])$: the conditional noise is $Z^n$ given $\sqrt{t/s}Z^n+\sqrt{1-t/s}W^n$. For a coordinate variance $p_j$, minimizing the quadratic residual variance of $U_j$ given $V_j$ gives $(1-t/s)(1+sp_j)/(1+tp_j)$. Step 1.1 therefore bounds the entropy difference by $\sum_j\log_2((1+sp_j)/(1+tp_j))$. This logarithmic ratio has derivative $(s-t)/((1+sp)(1+tp)\ln2)$, which is nonnegative and decreasing. Jensen and the average variance bound yield the first claimed inequality. If $s=t$ the two marginal entropies agree; if $t=0<s$ the same construction and computation apply. If $s=t=0$ both outputs are pure Gaussian noise.

Let $p_{i,j}=\operatorname{Var}(X_{i,j})$. The optimal scalar linear estimate of $Y_{1,j}$ from $S_{1,j}$ has residual variance $1+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j}+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,j}/(1+|h_{12}|^2p_{1,j})$: independence of the two user vectors and the noises eliminates all other covariances. Step 1.1 bounds the conditional entropy by the logarithm of this variance times $\pi e$. The map $x\mapsto x/(1+kx)$ is increasing and concave on $[0,\infty)$ for $k\ge0$, with second derivative $-2k/(1+kx)^3$; hence the residual variance is increasing and concave in the two powers, and its logarithm is also concave and increasing. Jensen and $n^{-1}\sum_jp_{i,j}\le P_i$ give the first conditional-output bound. Reflection gives the second. This calculation has no division by a channel gain and remains valid when any gain vanishes.

The output variances are $1+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,j}+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j}$ and $1+|h_{12}|^2p_{1,j}+|h_{22}|^2p_{2,j}$. Applying the coordinate chain rule, [F2], and logarithmic Jensen gives the two unconditioned-output bounds. Given $X_1^n$, subtract its contribution from $Y_2^n$; independence leaves the linear-estimation problem for $h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n$ from $h_{21}X_2^n+Z_1^n$. Its coordinate residual variance is $1+|h_{22}|^2p_{2,j}/(1+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j})$. The same concavity calculation proves the final conditional bound. Reflection proves its counterpart.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The two-user Gaussian interference channel has independent messages, separate encoders, and outputs
$$Y_1=h_{11}X_1+h_{21}X_2+Z_1,\qquad Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+Z_2.$$
For the **real model**, $X_i,h_{ji},Z_j$ are real and $Z_j\sim N(0,1)$. For the **complex model**, the inputs and gains are complex and $Z_j\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,1)$ with density $\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$. The receiver-noise variables are independent across receivers and channel uses and independent of the messages, so the channel is memoryless. Each power budget satisfies $P_i\ge0$. A length-$n$ code has independent uniform messages $M_i$ on $[m_i]$ for integers $m_i\ge1$, deterministic separate encoders $X_i^n=f_i(M_i)$, and decoders $\widehat M_i=g_i(Y_i^n)$; no feedback is present. The expected average-power constraints are $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[X_{i,t}^2]\le P_i$ in the real model and $n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E|X_{i,t}|^2\le P_i$ in the complex model, with expectations under the uniform message law. The average joint error is $\Pr\{(\widehat M_1,\widehat M_2)\ne(M_1,M_2)\}$. For either model define
$$\mathrm{SNR}_1=|h_{11}|^2P_1,\quad \mathrm{SNR}_2=|h_{22}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_1=|h_{21}|^2P_2,\quad \mathrm{INR}_2=|h_{12}|^2P_1.$$
Rates are bits per use, $R_i=n^{-1}\log_2m_i$. For a scalar unit-noise AWGN link $Y=aX+Z$ with power constraint $P$, the capacity is $\kappa\log_2(1+|a|^2P)$, attained by a centered real Gaussian input or a circular complex Gaussian input; $\kappa=1/2$ in the real model and $\kappa=1$ in the complex model.

Assume AC. Let $Z\in\mathbb C$ have a Lebesgue density, finite mean $\mu$, finite differential entropy, and positive-definite real covariance matrix $K$ for $(\operatorname{Re}Z,\operatorname{Im}Z)$. Put $\sigma^2=\mathbb E|Z-\mu|^2=\operatorname{tr}K$. Then
$$h(Z)\le\ln(\pi e\sigma^2).$$
Equality holds exactly for the circular complex Gaussian law $\mathcal{CN}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with density $(\pi\sigma^2)^{-1}\exp(-|z-\mu|^2/\sigma^2)$.

Let $f$ be a Lebesgue probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ with $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$ and $\int |x|^2f(x)\,dx<\infty$. Then $\int f(x)|\ln f(x)|\,dx<\infty$, so the differential entropy in [[def-it-real-differential-entropy]] is a finite real number.

Assume AC. Let $U,V,Y,S$ take values in standard-Borel spaces. Then
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(U;Y|S)+I(V;Y|U,S)$$
and also
$$I((U,V);Y|S)=I(V;Y|S)+I(U;Y|V,S),$$
where these are equalities of extended nonnegative quantities. In particular, if the conditional law of $Y$ given $(U,V,S)$ depends only on $(V,S)$, then
$$I(U;Y|S)\le I(V;Y|S).$$

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. For the absolutely continuous branch $P\ll P_E\otimes P_F$, assume AC as required by [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; the non-absolutely-continuous branch below remains $+\infty$. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

derivations.claim: If $(T,S)$ are Gaussian-smoothed finite-second-moment variables, then $h(T|S)=h(T-kS|S)\le h(T-kS)\le\log_2(\pi e\operatorname{Var}(T-kS))$ for every complex $k$. The first identity is conditional translation and the first inequality is conditional mutual-information nonnegativity; the second is [F2]. A finite-dimensional convolution with a nonsingular Gaussian has a density bounded by the peak of that Gaussian and finite second moment; [F3], applied after identifying complex vectors with real vectors, therefore makes every relevant joint, marginal, and residual differential entropy finite. In particular the pairs $(Y_1^n,S_1^n)$ and $(Y_2^n,S_2^n)$ have nonsingular independent receiver-noise coordinates, and the degraded pair below has nonsingular joint Gaussian noise when $s>t$. Their conditional entropies are differences of these finite joint and marginal entropies. For conditioning additionally on $X_1^n$, which need not have a density, first subtract its known translated contribution; independence removes that conditioning and leaves the nonsingular smoothed pair $(h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n,S_2^n)$. For a channel with conditional density $w(t|x)$ and positive output density $f_T(t)$, the joint-to-product density ratio is $w(t|x)/f_T(t)$. Thus [F5] gives $I(X;T)=\int\ln(w(t|x)/f_T(t))\,dP_{X,T}$. When $T=BX+Z$ with independent nonsingular Gaussian $Z$, the two log integrals are finite by [F3] and the quadratic Gaussian log density, and this integral equals $h(T)-h(Z)$. The same calculation with conditional densities justifies the conditional entropy identities used below, since their joint and marginal entropies are finite as established above. At zero signal power the same Gaussian density argument applies without alteration. Coordinate entropy chain rules give $h(T^n|S^n)\le\sum_j h(T_j|S_j)$.

Suppose $s>t$ and set $U^n=\sqrt{s}X^n+Z^n$, $V^n=\sqrt{t/s}\,U^n+\sqrt{1-t/s}\,W^n$. The marginal law of $V^n$ is the lower-SNR channel and $X^n-U^n-V^n$ is Markov. Thus the difference of the two output entropies equals $I(X^n;U^n|V^n)=h(U^n|V^n)-n\log_2(\pi e[1-t/s])$: the conditional noise is $Z^n$ given $\sqrt{t/s}Z^n+\sqrt{1-t/s}W^n$. For a coordinate variance $p_j$, minimizing the quadratic residual variance of $U_j$ given $V_j$ gives $(1-t/s)(1+sp_j)/(1+tp_j)$. Step 1.1 therefore bounds the entropy difference by $\sum_j\log_2((1+sp_j)/(1+tp_j))$. This logarithmic ratio has derivative $(s-t)/((1+sp)(1+tp)\ln2)$, which is nonnegative and decreasing. Jensen and the average variance bound yield the first claimed inequality. If $s=t$ the two marginal entropies agree; if $t=0<s$ the same construction and computation apply. If $s=t=0$ both outputs are pure Gaussian noise.

Let $p_{i,j}=\operatorname{Var}(X_{i,j})$. The optimal scalar linear estimate of $Y_{1,j}$ from $S_{1,j}$ has residual variance $1+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j}+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,j}/(1+|h_{12}|^2p_{1,j})$: independence of the two user vectors and the noises eliminates all other covariances. Step 1.1 bounds the conditional entropy by the logarithm of this variance times $\pi e$. The map $x\mapsto x/(1+kx)$ is increasing and concave on $[0,\infty)$ for $k\ge0$, with second derivative $-2k/(1+kx)^3$; hence the residual variance is increasing and concave in the two powers, and its logarithm is also concave and increasing. Jensen and $n^{-1}\sum_jp_{i,j}\le P_i$ give the first conditional-output bound. Reflection gives the second. This calculation has no division by a channel gain and remains valid when any gain vanishes.

The output variances are $1+|h_{11}|^2p_{1,j}+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j}$ and $1+|h_{12}|^2p_{1,j}+|h_{22}|^2p_{2,j}$. Applying the coordinate chain rule, [F2], and logarithmic Jensen gives the two unconditioned-output bounds. Given $X_1^n$, subtract its contribution from $Y_2^n$; independence leaves the linear-estimation problem for $h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n$ from $h_{21}X_2^n+Z_1^n$. Its coordinate residual variance is $1+|h_{22}|^2p_{2,j}/(1+|h_{21}|^2p_{2,j})$. The same concavity calculation proves the final conditional bound. Reflection proves its counterpart.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ take values in a finite nonempty set $S$ and let $Y$ take values in a standard-Borel space $(T,\mathcal T)$. Let $K:T\rightsquigarrow S$ be a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$, so that $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution given $\sigma(Y)$. Define
$$H(X\mid Y):=\int_T\left(-\sum_{x\in S}K(y,\{x\})\ln K(y,\{x\})\right)P_Y(dy),$$
with $0\ln0:=0$ and natural logarithms. The finite entropy convention is that of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]]. Each evaluation $y\mapsto K(y,\{x\})$ is measurable. The explicit argument in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]] proves $-t\ln t$ extends continuously to zero and is bounded by $1/e$ on $[0,1]$; hence the finite entropy integrand is measurable and bounded by $|S|/e$. The result is independent of the supplied version by simultaneous almost-everywhere uniqueness of standard-Borel regular conditional laws.

This definition permits a non-finite observation Y; only the target alphabet S is finite. If Y is finite, then for each positive-mass y the conditional-law identity gives $K(y,\{x\})P_Y(\{y\})=P(X=x,Y=y)$, so $K(y,\{x\})=p_{X|y}(x)$. Evaluating the integral as a finite weighted sum therefore gives exactly the convention of [[def-it-finite-conditional-entropy]], by [[cor-expectation-agrees-with-the-finite-weighted-sum]].

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

Assume AC for the countable determining-algebra supplier. If $K,L$ are regular conditional distributions of the same standard-Borel-valued random element $X$ given $\mathcal G$, there is one $N\in\mathcal G$ with $P(N)=0$ such that $K(\omega,\cdot)=L(\omega,\cdot)$ as measures for every $\omega\notin N$.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

derivations.claim: If two versions of the conditional law of $X$ given $Z$ are supplied, [F2] gives one $P_Z$-null set outside which their probability measures agree. Every atom probability, and hence the finite entropy sum in [F1], then agrees pointwise outside that set. Integrating gives the same $H(X\mid Z)$. The same argument applies to $(X,U)\mid Z$ and to $U\mid(X,Z)$.

Choose regular conditional laws of $(X,U)$ given $Z$ and of $U$ given $(X,Z)$; they exist by [A1, F3], since $(X,U)$ and $(X,Z)$ are standard Borel by [F4]. Write $p_{ij}(z)=P(X=i,U=j\mid Z=z)$, $p_i(z)=\sum_jp_{ij}(z)$, and $m_{ij}(z)=P(U=j\mid X=i,Z=z)$ for the chosen versions. The function $p_i$ is itself a conditional law of $X$ given $Z$, so [F2] makes it agree almost everywhere with the version used in $H(X\mid Z)$. For each $i,j$ and measurable $C$ in the value space of $Z$, the two disintegrations [F3] give $$\int_C p_i(z)m_{ij}(z)\,P_Z(dz)=P(X=i,U=j,Z\in C)=\int_Cp_{ij}(z)\,P_Z(dz).$$ Both integrands are bounded and measurable. Testing the sets where one exceeds the other by at least $1/n$, for each $n\ge1$, shows $p_i(z)m_{ij}(z)=p_{ij}(z)$ almost everywhere; because the alphabets are finite, one null set works for every $i,j$.

Outside that null set, if $p_i(z)=0$ then every $p_{ij}(z)=0$, so the row contributes zero to the conditional entropy. If $p_i(z)>0$, then $m_{ij}(z)=p_{ij}(z)/p_i(z)$ for every $j$. On positive entries, $\ln p_{ij}=\ln p_i+\ln m_{ij}$; multiplying by $-p_{ij}$ and summing over the finite alphabets gives $$H(X,U\mid Z=z)=H(X\mid Z=z)+\sum_i p_i(z)H(U\mid X=i,Z=z).$$

Integrate the finite conditional identity from step 2.1 with respect to $P_Z$. The disintegration identity [F3] identifies the last integral with $H(U\mid X,Z)$ and the other terms with their definitions. By the bound $-t\ln t\le1/e$ in [F1], each conditional entropy is bounded by its finite alphabet size divided by $e$, so all integrals are finite and no subtraction of infinite quantities occurs. Step 1.1 proves the accompanying version-independence assertion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

Assume AC. Let X,Y,Z be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces and write $P_{ZXY}$ for the joint law of $(Z,X,Y)$ in that coordinate order. Let $K(z,\cdot)$ and $L(z,\cdot)$ be regular conditional laws of X and Y given Z=z. Let R be the probability law on the same product space whose rectangle values are
$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz).$$
Its existence, uniqueness, and independence of the versions K,L are established in [[lem-same-marginal-conditional-product-law-well-defined]]. Define the **conditional mutual information** by
$$I(X;Y\mid Z):=D(P_{ZXY}\|R)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The reference R has the same Z marginal as the joint law and makes X,Y independent conditionally on Z. The logarithm is natural, so finite values are measured in nats under [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The definition is a divergence between full probability laws; it does not subtract two possibly infinite entropies.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC. For nonnegative measurable $X_n$, $E[\liminf_n X_n\mid\mathcal G]\le\liminf_n E[X_n\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely, in the extended sense. If real-valued measurable $X_n$ and $X$ satisfy $X_n\to X$ almost surely and $|X_n|\le W$ almost surely for one nonnegative $W\in L^1(P)$, then $E[X_n\mid\mathcal G]\to E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely and in $L^1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

derivations.claim: By [F2] and [F1], $I(X;Y)=0$ exactly when $P_{XY}=P_X\otimes P_Y$, which is the stated independence condition.
By [F3] and [F1], $I(X;Y\mid Z)=0$ exactly when the joint law $P_{ZXY}$ of $(Z,X,Y)$ equals the conditional-product reference law R.

Suppose $P_{ZXY}=R$, using the coordinate order $(Z,X,Y)$ of [F3]. For all measurable A,B,C the rectangle formula for R gives $P(X\in A,Y\in B,Z\in C)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)P_Z(dz).$ By the regular conditional law identities, $K(Z,A)$ and $L(Z,B)$ are versions of the two conditional expectations in [F4]. The displayed identity says their product is the conditional-expectation version of $\mathbf1_{\{X\in A,Y\in B\}}$ by [F5]. Thus [F4] holds for indicators. Linearity gives it for bounded simple functions; bounded measurable functions follow by bounded simple approximation and [F6]. Conversely, [F4] applied to indicators gives the same rectangle identity, so $P_{ZXY}$ and R agree on every rectangle $C\times A\times B$. These rectangles determine the probability law by [F7], hence $P_{ZXY}=R$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ has a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures: if finite measures $\mu,\nu$ agree on $\mathcal A$, then $\mu=\nu$. In particular it determines probability measures.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on one measurable space. For bounded measurable real $f$, put
$$\Phi_{P,Q}(f):=\int f\,dP-\ln\int e^f\,dQ.$$
Then
$$D(P\|Q)=\sup_{f\ {\rm bounded\ measurable}}\Phi_{P,Q}(f).$$
Equivalently, for every finite measurable partition $\mathcal P=(A_1,\ldots,A_m)$ of the whole space,
$$D(P\|Q)=\sup_{\mathcal P}\sum_{i=1}^m P(A_i)\ln\frac{P(A_i)}{Q(A_i)},$$
where $0\ln(0/q)=0$ and a term with $P(A_i)>0=Q(A_i)$ is $+\infty$. The result includes singular and infinite-divergence cases.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

Let X,Y,Z be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces and joint law $P_{XYZ}$. Let $K(z,\cdot)$ and $L(z,\cdot)$ be regular conditional laws of X and Y given Z=z. Let R be the probability law on the product space whose rectangle values are
$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz).$$
Its existence, uniqueness, and independence of the versions K,L are established in [[lem-same-marginal-conditional-product-law-well-defined]]. Define the **conditional mutual information** by
$$I(X;Y\mid Z):=D(P_{XYZ}\|R)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The reference R has the same Z marginal as the joint law and makes X,Y independent conditionally on Z. The logarithm is natural, so finite values are measured in nats under [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The definition is a divergence between full probability laws; it does not subtract two possibly infinite entropies.

Let $X,Y,Z$ be random elements with standard-Borel value spaces, and let $K(z,\cdot)$ and $L(z,\cdot)$ be supplied conditional laws of $X$ and $Y$ given $Z=z$. The product kernels $M(z,\cdot)=K(z,\cdot)\otimes L(z,\cdot)$ form a probability kernel. The joint law
$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz)$$
exists uniquely on the product sigma-algebra and does not depend on the chosen versions of $K,L$. It has $Z$ marginal $P_Z$ and conditional law $M$ for $(X,Y)$ given $Z$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: Let $(\mathcal G_n)$ be any increasing sequence of sub-sigma-algebras generating $\mathcal G$, and let $\rho=P+Q$ for probability measures on $\mathcal G$. The union $\mathcal U=\bigcup_n\mathcal G_n$ is an algebra. The class of $A\in\mathcal G$ approximable in $\rho$-measure by a set in $\mathcal U$ is a sigma-algebra: complements preserve the symmetric-difference measure, finite unions preserve approximation, and for a countable union one first truncates it using continuity from below [F5] of the finite measure $\rho$, then approximates the finite union. Hence every set in $\mathcal G$ is approximable. Approximating bounded measurable functions first by simple functions and then their level sets gives bounded $\mathcal U$-measurable functions converging in $L^1(\rho)$, with one $\mathcal G_n$ containing each finite simple approximation. The approximants may be clipped to the same bound M. On that bound, [F2]'s variational functional is continuous under $L^1(\rho)$ approximation: $e^t$ is Lipschitz on $[-M,M]$, and the exponential integral is bounded below by $e^{-M}$. By [F2] applied to $P,Q$ and their restrictions to each $\mathcal G_n$, the supremum over all bounded $\mathcal G_n$-measurable functions is $D(P|_{\mathcal G_n}\|Q|_{\mathcal G_n})$. These test classes increase, so the restricted divergences increase; the approximation shows their supremum equals the unrestricted variational supremum $D(P\|Q)$. Hence $D(P\|Q)=\lim_n D(P|_{\mathcal G_n}\|Q|_{\mathcal G_n})$.

By [F1], countable generating algebras exist; their first-n finite Boolean subalgebras yield increasing finite quantizers by labeling their atoms. For the quantizers in the Statement, the same generated-sigma property is assumed, so in either case $\sigma(q_n(X),r_n(Y))$ increases to the product sigma-algebra of $(X,Y)$. Under the map $(x,y)\mapsto(q_n(x),r_n(y))$, the push-forward of $P_X\otimes P_Y$ is $P_{q_n(X)}\otimes P_{r_n(Y)}$, as is checked on rectangles of the finite output sets. Since $\sigma(q_n(X),r_n(Y))$ consists exactly of preimages of output events, every bounded measurable test function on that sigma-algebra factors through the finite output map. Therefore its restricted KL equals the KL of the push-forward laws, which by [F3] is $I(q_n(X);r_n(Y))$. Applying step 1.1 proves the ordinary mutual-information limit.

For the conditional statement, put $\mathcal G_n=\sigma(Z,q_n(X),r_n(Y))$. These sigma-algebras increase to the full product sigma-algebra of $(Z,X,Y)$ because the entire Z sigma-algebra is retained. A bounded $\mathcal G_n$-measurable simple function factors through $(Z,q_n(X),r_n(Y))$: each level set is the preimage of a measurable output set, and finitely many output sets can be made disjoint without changing their preimages. Uniform simple approximation extends this factorization to all bounded variational test functions. Hence the KL restricted to $\mathcal G_n$ equals the KL between the push-forward joint and reference laws. By rectangle uniqueness, this is exactly the conditional-product reference law for the quantized variables. Step 1.1 therefore gives the conditional limit.
Steps 2.1 and 2.2 establish both limits. The proof quantizes X and Y only; it makes no claim that coarsening Z decreases conditional mutual information.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

Assume AC only for the interface to the published general definition [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Let $p,q$ be probability vectors on a finite set $S$, and let $P(A)=\sum_{i\in A}p_i$, $Q(A)=\sum_{i\in A}q_i$ on $\mathcal P(S)$. Then the measurable-space divergence $D(P\|Q)$ equals the finite KL sum $\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i)$, with value $+\infty$ exactly when some $p_i>0=q_i$.

Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm $\log$ of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Unless a base is displayed, every information quantity on this page uses $\ln$ and is measured in **nats**. For a base $b>1$ and $t>0$, define
$$\log_b t:=\frac{\ln t}{\ln b}.$$
The denominator is positive: $b>1$, $\ln$ is strictly increasing, and $\ln 1=0$ by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]. A base-$b$ entropy or divergence is obtained by replacing each $\ln$ in the finite formulas below by $\log_b$; use $0\log_b0:=0$ and assign $+\infty$ to a positive numerator over a zero denominator. The case $b=2$ measures **bits**; $b=e$ gives nats.

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

derivations.claim: On $\{0,1\}$, define $d(x,y)=0$ if $x=y$ and $d(x,y)=1$ otherwise; distinct endpoints force at least one of the two intermediate distances to be 1, so the triangle inequality holds. For a Cauchy sequence, tolerance $1/2$ forces all sufficiently late terms to be equal, so the metric is complete. The finite set itself is a finite dense subset, and radius-$1/2$ balls are singletons, so the topology is discrete. By the definitions in [F4], this is a Polish presentation of the discrete sigma-algebra, which is therefore standard Borel. If $p=0$ or $p=1$, X and Y are the same constant almost surely; their joint law and the product of their marginals are the same point mass. Thus [F1] gives a finite-alphabet mutual information, [F2] gives $I(X;Y)=0$, and [F3] gives the same entropy.

Suppose $0<p<1$. The joint law of $(X,Y)$ has masses $p$ at $(1,1)$ and $1-p$ at $(0,0)$, and zero elsewhere. The product law has masses $p^2$ at $(1,1)$ and $(1-p)^2$ at $(0,0)$. By [F1]–[F2], $I(X;Y)=p\ln\frac{p}{p^2}+(1-p)\ln\frac{1-p}{(1-p)^2}=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p).$ The last quantity is $H(X)$ by [F3].
The endpoint cases in step 1.1 and the interior case in step 2.1 exhaust $p\in[0,1]$ and establish the claimed identity throughout.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be measurable spaces and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(E\times F,\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$. Its marginals are $P_E(A)=P(A\times F)$ and $P_F(B)=P(E\times B)$. The product probability $P_E\otimes P_F$ exists by the finite product-measure theorem. For the absolutely continuous branch $P\ll P_E\otimes P_F$, assume AC as required by [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]; the non-absolutely-continuous branch below remains $+\infty$. Define the **measure-theoretic mutual information** of the joint law $P$ by
$$I(P):=D(P\|P_E\otimes P_F)\in[0,+\infty].$$
For random elements $X,Y$ with joint law $P_{XY}$, write $I(X;Y):=I(P_{XY})$. The logarithm convention is the natural logarithm, so finite values are in nats as fixed by [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The divergence is directional in its two law arguments and is $+\infty$ when $P_{XY}\not\ll P_X\otimes P_Y$.

This definition uses only the joint law, not a choice of density or a difference of entropy quantities.

Let $p_{XY}$ be a joint probability vector on finite alphabets $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, with marginals $p_X(x):=\sum_y p_{XY}(x,y)$ and $p_Y(y):=\sum_xp_{XY}(x,y)$. The marginals are probability vectors by [[lem-it-finite-marginals-and-conditionals-are-pmfs]]. The joint vector is the outcome-weight function of the canonical finite probability space from [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]; its coordinate maps are finite random elements in the sense of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Define mutual information in nats by

$$I(X;Y):=D(p_{XY}\|p_X\otimes p_Y)=\sum_{(x,y):p_{XY}(x,y)>0}p_{XY}(x,y)\ln\frac{p_{XY}(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)},$$

where $D$ is the finite KL convention of [[def-qa-35-finite-probability-entropy-and-stochastic-matrices]] and $(p_X\otimes p_Y)(x,y):=p_X(x)p_Y(y)$. Every ratio in the displayed sum is positive and finite: if $p_{XY}(x,y)>0$, then each marginal sum is at least that positive entry. The sum is over finite support, so $I(X;Y)$ is finite. The base-$b$ version replaces $\ln$ by $\log_b$.

Assume AC only for the interface to the published general definition [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Let $p,q$ be probability vectors on a finite set $S$, and let $P(A)=\sum_{i\in A}p_i$, $Q(A)=\sum_{i\in A}q_i$ on $\mathcal P(S)$. Then the measurable-space divergence $D(P\|Q)$ equals the finite KL sum $\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i)$, with value $+\infty$ exactly when some $p_i>0=q_i$.

Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm $\log$ of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Unless a base is displayed, every information quantity on this page uses $\ln$ and is measured in **nats**. For a base $b>1$ and $t>0$, define
$$\log_b t:=\frac{\ln t}{\ln b}.$$
The denominator is positive: $b>1$, $\ln$ is strictly increasing, and $\ln 1=0$ by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]. A base-$b$ entropy or divergence is obtained by replacing each $\ln$ in the finite formulas below by $\log_b$; use $0\log_b0:=0$ and assign $+\infty$ to a positive numerator over a zero denominator. The case $b=2$ measures **bits**; $b=e$ gives nats.

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

derivations.claim: On $\{0,1\}$, define $d(x,y)=0$ if $x=y$ and $d(x,y)=1$ otherwise; distinct endpoints force at least one of the two intermediate distances to be 1, so the triangle inequality holds. For a Cauchy sequence, tolerance $1/2$ forces all sufficiently late terms to be equal, so the metric is complete. The finite set itself is a finite dense subset, and radius-$1/2$ balls are singletons, so the topology is discrete. By the definitions in [F4], this is a Polish presentation of the discrete sigma-algebra, which is therefore standard Borel. If $p=0$ or $p=1$, X and Y are the same constant almost surely; their joint law and the product of their marginals are the same point mass. Thus [F1] gives a finite-alphabet mutual information, [F2] gives $I(X;Y)=0$, and [F3] gives the same entropy.

Suppose $0<p<1$. The joint law of $(X,Y)$ has masses $p$ at $(1,1)$ and $1-p$ at $(0,0)$, and zero elsewhere. The product law has masses $p^2$ at $(1,1)$ and $(1-p)^2$ at $(0,0)$. By [F1]–[F2], $I(X;Y)=p\ln\frac{p}{p^2}+(1-p)\ln\frac{1-p}{(1-p)^2}=-p\ln p-(1-p)\ln(1-p).$ The last quantity is $H(X)$ by [F3].
The endpoint cases in step 1.1 and the interior case in step 2.1 exhaust $p\in[0,1]$ and establish the claimed identity throughout.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).
Let $I=[0,1]$ with the subspace topology from the usual real topology and with its Borel sigma-algebra. Then $(I,\mathcal B(I))$ is a standard-Borel space ([[def-standard-borel-space]]).

For a random element $X$ with law $P_X$, define its **law entropy** by
$$H(X):=I(X;X)=D(P_{XX}\|P_X\otimes P_X),$$
where $P_{XX}$ is the joint law of the diagonal pair $(X,X)$. This is an extended nonnegative quantity in nats and depends only on the law of X.

Let X have a probability law P on a standard-Borel space. Let $S=\{x:P(\{x\})>0\}$ be its set of atoms. Then S is countable. If $P(S)=1$ and its atom masses are $(p_i)$, the law entropy from [[def-law-entropy-as-self-mutual-information]] is
$$H(X)=\sum_i p_i\ln\frac1{p_i},$$
with value $+\infty$ allowed. If $P(S)<1$, then $H(X)=+\infty$.

For a probability law with Lebesgue density $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$, its **differential entropy**, when the integral is defined, is
$$h(f):=-\int_{\mathbb R^d} f(x)\ln f(x)\,dx.$$
This density-based quantity is not the law entropy $H(X)=I(X;X)$ of [[def-law-entropy-as-self-mutual-information]]. Differential entropy may be finite or negative even when law entropy is infinite; the uniform law on $[0,1]$ is a basic example. No identity between the two is used in this page.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

where $P_{XX}$ is the joint law of the diagonal pair $(X,X)$. This is an extended nonnegative quantity in nats and depends only on the law of X.

Let X have a probability law P on a standard-Borel space. Let $S=\{x:P(\{x\})>0\}$ be its set of atoms. Then S is countable. If $P(S)=1$ and its atom masses are $(p_i)$, the law entropy from [[def-law-entropy-as-self-mutual-information]] is
$$H(X)=\sum_i p_i\ln\frac1{p_i},$$
with value $+\infty$ allowed. If $P(S)<1$, then $H(X)=+\infty$.

For a probability law with Lebesgue density $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$, its **differential entropy**, when the integral is defined, is
$$h(f):=-\int_{\mathbb R^d} f(x)\ln f(x)\,dx.$$
This density-based quantity is not the law entropy $H(X)=I(X;X)$ of [[def-law-entropy-as-self-mutual-information]]. Differential entropy may be finite or negative even when law entropy is infinite; the uniform law on $[0,1]$ is a basic example. No identity between the two is used in this page.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;

Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional complex inner-product space with $d\ge1$. Form the orthogonal direct sum $B:=A\oplus\mathbb C e$, where $e$ is a unit erasure vector orthogonal to every vector in $A$; the inner product on pairs is $\langle(x,a),(y,b)\rangle_B=\langle x,y\rangle_A+a\overline b$. Thus $\dim B=d+1$ by [[cor-dimension-of-a-direct-sum]]. Let $J:A\to B$ be the isometric inclusion into the data summand.

For an erasure probability $\epsilon\in[0,1]$, the **$d$-dimensional quantum erasure channel** is the linear map

$$\mathcal E_{d,\epsilon}(X):=(1-\epsilon)JXJ^*+ \epsilon\operatorname{tr}(X)|e\rangle\langle e|,\qquad X\in\mathcal L(A).$$

For a density operator $\rho$, this outputs the data state with probability $1-\epsilon$ and the orthogonal erasure flag with probability $\epsilon$. The definition is on the full operator space, and its channel property is established in [[thm-it-qudit-erasure-channel-is-cptp]].

Let $\mathcal N:A\to B$ be a finite-dimensional channel and fix a complementary channel $\mathcal N^c:A\to E$ coming from one finite Stinespring isometry. Relative to this chosen dilation, $\mathcal N$ is **degradable** if there exists a quantum channel $\mathcal D:B\to E$ such that

$$\mathcal N^c=\mathcal D\circ\mathcal N.$$

It is **antidegradable** relative to this dilation if there exists a quantum channel $\mathcal A:E\to B$ such that

$$\mathcal N=\mathcal A\circ\mathcal N^c.$$

All hypotheses and conclusions below use the same fixed complementary dilation and the corresponding degrading or antidegrading channel.
For every integer $d\ge1$ and $\epsilon\in[0,1]$, the map $\mathcal E_{d,\epsilon}$ defined in [[def-it-qudit-erasure-channel]] is a finite-dimensional quantum channel.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ have a finite Kraus representation
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger$. Then $\Phi$ is completely positive.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

derivations.claim: Use the isometry $V_\epsilon x=\sqrt{1-\epsilon}J_Bx\otimes e_E+\sqrt\epsilon e\otimes J_Ex$ from the proof of [[thm-it-qudit-erasure-channel-is-cptp]]. Tracing the first factor $B$ leaves the data block $\epsilon J_EXJ_E^*$ and the flag block $(1-\epsilon)\operatorname{tr}(X)|e_E\rangle\langle e_E|$; the cross terms vanish because the data and erasure subspaces are orthogonal. The data block precedes the flag block because $E=A\oplus\mathbb C e_E$.

Suppose $0\le\epsilon\le\tfrac12$ and set $\alpha=\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)\in[0,1]$. Choose an orthonormal basis $(u_j)_{j<d}$ of the data summand of $B$, and define the finite Kraus family from $B$ to $E$ by $K_0=\sqrt\alpha J_EJ_B^*$, $K_j=\sqrt{1-\alpha}|e_E\rangle\langle u_j|$ for $j<d$, and $K_e=|e_E\rangle\langle e_B|$. The sum of adjoint products is $\alpha\Pi_A+(1-\alpha)\Pi_A+|e_B\rangle\langle e_B|=I_B$, so the induced map $\mathcal D_\epsilon(X)=\sum KXK^*$ is a channel by [F4]–[F6]. On an erasure-channel output, its data block has weight $\alpha(1-\epsilon)X=\epsilon X$ and its flag block has weight $[(1-\alpha)(1-\epsilon)+\epsilon]\operatorname{tr}(X)=(1-\epsilon)\operatorname{tr}(X)$. Thus $\mathcal D_\epsilon\mathcal E_{d,\epsilon}=\mathcal E^c_{d,\epsilon}$, proving degradability.

Suppose $\tfrac12\le\epsilon\le1$ and set $\beta=(1-\epsilon)/\epsilon\in[0,1]$. Choose an orthonormal basis $(u_j^E)_{j<d}$ of the data summand of $E$ and define a finite Kraus family from $E$ to $B$ by $L_0=\sqrt\beta J_BJ_E^*$, $L_j=\sqrt{1-\beta}|e_B\rangle\langle u_j^E|$ for $j<d$, and $L_e=|e_B\rangle\langle e_E|$. Its adjoint products sum to $I_E$, so its Kraus map $\mathcal A_\epsilon$ is a channel by [F4]–[F6]. Applying it to the complement in step 1.1 gives data weight $\beta\epsilon X=(1-\epsilon)X$ and erasure-flag weight $[(1-\beta)\epsilon+(1-\epsilon)]\operatorname{tr}(X)=\epsilon\operatorname{tr}(X)$. Hence $\mathcal A_\epsilon\mathcal E^c_{d,\epsilon}=\mathcal E_{d,\epsilon}$, proving antidegradability. At $\epsilon=\tfrac12$ both parameters equal one and both relations hold.

Let $A$ and $B$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $\mathcal N:\mathcal L(A)\to\mathcal L(B)$ be a quantum channel as in [[def-qc-quantum-channel]]. Choose a finite-dimensional environment $E$ and a linear isometry $V:A\to B\otimes E$ such that

$$\mathcal N(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^*)$$

for every $X\in\mathcal L(A)$; such a dilation exists by [[thm-qc-finite-stinespring-dilation]]. The channel

$$\mathcal N^c(X):=\operatorname{Tr}_B(VXV^*)\in\mathcal L(E)$$

is the **complementary channel associated with this chosen dilation**. The partial trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ contracts the first factor of the ordered product $B\otimes E$ ([[def-qc-first-factor-partial-trace]]).

It is a quantum channel: reorder $B\otimes E$ to $E\otimes B$ by the finite wire-permutation unitary ([[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], [[thm-qc-wire-permutation-is-unitary]]); the reordered $V$ is still an isometry, so tracing its second factor $B$ gives a channel by [[thm-qc-isometry-partial-trace-is-channel]].

Its **coherent information** from $A$ to $B$ is

$$I_c(\rho,\mathcal N):=S(\mathcal N(\rho))-S(\omega_{BR}),$$

where $S$ is finite-dimensional von Neumann entropy in nats ([[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]]). The value does not depend on the chosen purification: after padding reference spaces, any two purifications differ by a unitary on $R$ ([[thm-qc-purification-existence-and-unitary-equivalence]]); applying $\mathcal N\otimes\operatorname{id}_R$ preserves that unitary relation. A unitary maps an orthonormal eigenbasis to an orthonormal eigenbasis with the same eigenvalues, so entropy is unchanged ([[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]]). Padding adds only zero eigenvalues, which do not contribute.

consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

The right-hand side is independent of the chosen Stinespring dilation, since it equals the purification-defined quantity in [[def-it-quantum-channel-complement-and-coherent-information]].

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

For each count vector $t=(n_1,\ldots,n_d)$ with $\sum_j n_j=n$, let $m_t$ be the number of product basis words of that type, $p_t=m_t\prod_{j:n_j>0}\lambda_j^{n_j}$ (zero if any such $\lambda_j=0$), and omit types with $p_t=0$. Let $P_t$ project onto the span of the words of type $t$ and set $\tau_t=P_t/m_t$. These states are flat, their supports are mutually orthogonal, and $$\rho^{\otimes n}=\sum_{t:p_t>0}p_t\tau_t.$$ There are at most $(n+1)^d$ types. If $N_T$ is their number and $u$ is the uniform law on them, [F6] gives $0\le D(p\|u)=\ln N_T-H(T)$, so $H(T)\le d\ln(n+1)$. Since $S(\tau_t)=\ln m_t$, the logarithm product law [F5] and $\sum_t p_t n_j=n\lambda_j$ yield $$\sum_t p_tS(\tau_t)=\sum_t p_t\ln m_t=nS(\rho)-H(T).$$

Let $B_t=\mathcal N^{\otimes n}(\tau_t)$ and $E_t=(\mathcal N^c)^{\otimes n}(\tau_t)$, with averages $\bar B=\sum_tp_tB_t=\mathcal N(\rho)^{\otimes n}$ and $\bar E=\sum_tp_tE_t=\mathcal N^c(\rho)^{\otimes n}$. By [F4], the receiver-minus-environment entropy identity applies to each type. The lower mixture bound [F1] gives $\sum_tp_tS(B_t)\ge S(\bar B)-H(T)$, while its upper bound gives $\sum_tp_tS(E_t)\le S(\bar E)$. Product spectral decompositions and [F5] give $S(\bar B)-S(\bar E)=n[S(\mathcal N(\rho))-S(\mathcal N^c(\rho))]=nI_c(\rho,\mathcal N)$. Hence $$\sum_tp_t I_c(\tau_t,\mathcal N^{\otimes n})\ge nI_c(\rho,\mathcal N)-H(T).$$ Adding $\sum_tp_tS(\tau_t)=nS(\rho)-H(T)$ from step 1.1 gives the second inequality.

Each displayed left side in step 2.1 is an average over the finite positive-probability types, so at least one type attains at least the corresponding average lower bound. These are exact finite-$n$ estimates; no replacement of fixed-dimensional continuity by a uniform bound is involved.
