Fix a finite-input cq channel as in [[def-it-classical-quantum-memoryless-channel]]. For integers $n,M\ge1$, an $(n,M)$ **cq block code** consists of a deterministic encoder $m\mapsto x^n(m)\in\mathcal X^n$ for $m\in[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ and a finite POVM ([[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]) $(\Lambda_m)_{m\in[M]}$ on $H_B^{\otimes n}$. Under a uniform message, its **average block error** is
$$e_n:=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\left(1-\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda_m\rho_{x^n(m)})\right).$$
Its rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$ nats per channel use, using the natural-log unit convention of [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]]. A sequence of such codes is reliable if $e_n\to0$. The **classical capacity** $C_{\rm cq}$ is the supremum of $\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n$ over reliable sequences.

For each transmitted state, the POVM outcome weights sum to one by [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]], so $e_n$ is the uniform-message block error probability.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty classical label set, represented by a register $H_X$ with computational orthonormal basis $(\xi_x)_{x\in X}$ ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). For each $x$, write $\Pi_xz:=\langle z,\xi_x\rangle\xi_x$, the rank-one orthogonal projection using the root linear-first convention, as in [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Let $H_B$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. A finite **classical-quantum state** is

$$\rho_{XB}:=\sum_{x\in X}p_x\Pi_x\otimes\rho_x,$$

where $p_x\ge0$, $\sum_xp_x=1$, and each $\rho_x$ is a density operator on $H_B$. It is a density operator by [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Its quantum marginal is $\bar\rho_B:=\sum_xp_x\rho_x=\operatorname{Tr}_X\rho_{XB}$ by the second-factor partial-trace formula in [[def-qc-partial-trace]], and it is a density operator by [[lem-it-partial-traces-of-a-state-are-states]]. The **Holevo information** of this ensemble is

$$\chi(\{p_x,\rho_x\}_{x\in X}):=S(\bar\rho_B)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x),$$

where zero-probability branches contribute nothing. This is measured in nats under [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]].

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $(p_x)$ be a probability vector, let $\rho_x$ be density operators on a nonzero finite-dimensional space $H_B$, and let $\bar\rho:=\sum_xp_x\rho_x$. For a finite POVM $(E_y)_{y\in Y}$ on $H_B$, define $w(y\mid x):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_xE_y)$, $q_y:=\sum_xp_xw(y\mid x)$, and the classical mutual information

$$I(X:Y):=\sum_{x,y:p_xw(y\mid x)>0}p_xw(y\mid x)\ln\frac{w(y\mid x)}{q_y}.$$

Then

$$I(X:Y)\le\chi(\{p_x,\rho_x\})=S(\bar\rho)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x).$$

All logarithms are natural. First, for every density operator $\rho$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional space and every $\delta>0$, there are spectral projectors $\Pi_n$ for $\rho^{\otimes n}$ such that, as $n\to\infty$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_n\rho^{\otimes n})\to1,\qquad \operatorname{rank}\Pi_n\le e^{n(S(\rho)+\delta)},\qquad \Pi_n\rho^{\otimes n}\Pi_n\preceq e^{-n(S(\rho)-\delta)}\Pi_n.$$

Second, let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ be a probability vector, and let $\sigma_x$ be density operators on a nonzero finite-dimensional output space. Put $\bar\sigma=\sum_xp_x\sigma_x$ and $H(B|X)=\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\sigma_x)$. For every $\delta>0$, there are sets $T_n\subseteq\mathcal X^n$ with $p^{\otimes n}(T_n)\to1$, global spectral projectors $\Pi_n$ for $\bar\sigma^{\otimes n}$, and conditional spectral projectors $\Pi_{x^n}$ for $\bigotimes_i\sigma_{x_i}$, such that one sequence $u_n\to0$ satisfies, for every sufficiently large $n$ and every $x^n\in T_n$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_n\bar\sigma^{\otimes n})\to1,\quad \operatorname{tr}(\Pi_n\bigotimes_i\sigma_{x_i})\ge1-u_n,\quad \operatorname{tr}(\Pi_{x^n}\bigotimes_i\sigma_{x_i})\ge1-u_n,$$
$$\operatorname{rank}\Pi_n\le e^{n(S(\bar\sigma)+\delta)},\quad \Pi_n\bar\sigma^{\otimes n}\Pi_n\preceq e^{-n(S(\bar\sigma)-\delta)}\Pi_n,$$
$$\operatorname{rank}\Pi_{x^n}\le e^{n(H(B|X)+\delta)},\quad \Pi_{x^n}\left(\bigotimes_i\sigma_{x_i}\right)\Pi_{x^n}\preceq e^{-n(H(B|X)-\delta)}\Pi_{x^n}.$$
Zero eigenvalues are omitted from surprisal sums. No identical-distribution assumption is made for the conditional eigenbasis measurements.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $p$ be a probability vector, and let $\sigma_x$ be density operators on a finite-dimensional $H$. Let $\bar\sigma=\sum_xp_x\sigma_x$. Suppose that for every $x$ in the support of $p$, projections $\Pi,\Pi_x$ satisfy
$$\operatorname{tr}(\Pi\sigma_x)\ge1-u,\quad \operatorname{tr}(\Pi_x\sigma_x)\ge1-u,\quad \operatorname{rank}\Pi_x\le d,$$
and $\Pi\bar\sigma\Pi\preceq D^{-1}\Pi$, where $u\in[0,1]$ and $d,D>0$. For $M\ge1$, draw $X_1,\ldots,X_M$ independently with law $p$. Then the square-root POVM built from $\Gamma_m=\Pi\Pi_{X_m}\Pi$ has expected average error at most
$$2(u+2\sqrt{u})+4(M-1)\frac dD.$$

Let $H_A,H_B,H_C$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $\rho_{ABC}$ be a density operator on their ordered tensor product. Write $\rho_{AB},\rho_{BC},\rho_B$ for its marginals using the partial traces in [[def-qc-partial-trace]]. Then
$$S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})\ge S(\rho_B)+S(\rho_{ABC}),$$
where $S(\rho)=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho)$ with $0\ln0:=0$ as in [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]].

For each fixed finite dimension $d$, von Neumann entropy is continuous on density operators ([[def-qc-density-operator]]) on $\mathbb C^d$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]). Thus, if $\rho_k\to\rho$ in operator norm, then $S(\rho_k)\to S(\rho)$.

Let $X$ take values in an alphabet $\mathcal X$ of size $m\ge2$, let $Y$ be finite, and let $\widehat X$ be an estimator in the same alphabet generated from $Y$, so the joint pmf factors as $p_{XY\widehat X}=p_{XY}p_{\widehat X|Y}$. Put $P_e=\mathbb P[\widehat X\ne X]$ and define

$$h_2(t):=-t\ln t-(1-t)\ln(1-t),\qquad 0\ln0:=0.$$

Then

$$H(X|Y)\le h_2(P_e)+P_e\ln(m-1)\le \ln2+P_e\ln m.$$

For $m=1$, $X$ is constant and $H(X|Y)=0$.

For finite $X,Y,Z$ with a joint pmf,

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

derivations.claim: Write $\chi_*=\sup_{p\in\Delta(\mathcal X)}\chi_p$. The simplex is nonempty, closed, and bounded. For each state $\rho_x$, [F12] diagonalizes it with nonnegative eigenvalues summing to one by [F16], so its action on a unit vector has norm at most one and [F15] gives $\|\rho_x\|\le1$. Therefore $\|\bar\rho_p-\bar\rho_q\|\le\sum_x|p_x-q_x|$. Fix an orthonormal basis identifying $H_B$ unitarily with $\mathbb C^{\dim H_B}$; this preserves spectra and operator norm, so [F7] applies. Thus the first entropy term in $\chi_p$ is continuous in $p$; the second is a finite linear sum. Thus [F14] shows the supremum is attained, so $\chi_*=\max_p\chi_p$. A point-mass input law gives $\chi_p=0$ by [F2], hence $\chi_*\ge0$.

Fix $p$ and $0<R<\chi_p$. Choose $\delta>0$ with $R<\chi_p-2\delta$. Let $T_n$ be the input typical set from [F4], with excluded probability $\eta_n\to0$. Since $\eta_n\to0$, $p^{\otimes n}(T_n)=1-\eta_n>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$; for each earlier blocklength choose a fixed $x_0\in\mathcal X$ and use the one-message code with word $x_0^n$ and decoding POVM $\{I\}$. Draw each large-$n$ codeword independently from $p^{\otimes n}$ conditioned on $T_n$. Its mean output state is $$\bar\sigma_n'=\mathbb E[\rho_{X^n}\mid X^n\in T_n]\preceq(1-\eta_n)^{-1}\bar\rho_p^{\otimes n},\qquad \bar\rho_p=\sum_xp_x\rho_x.$$ The global typical projector from [F4] therefore obeys $\Pi_n\bar\sigma_n'\Pi_n\preceq(1-\eta_n)^{-1}e^{-n(S(\bar\rho_p)-\delta)}\Pi_n$. Each conditional projector has acceptance at least $1-u_n$, rank at most $e^{n(H(B|X)+\delta)}$, and the global projector accepts every conditioned codeword with at least $1-u_n$, where $u_n\to0$ and $H(B|X)=\sum_xp_xS(\rho_x)$.

Consider any $(n,M)$ code with $M\ge2$, uniform message $J$, output states $\omega_m=\bigotimes_i\rho_{x_i(m)}$, decoding outcome $\widehat J$, and average error $e$. The Holevo measurement bound [F3] gives $I(J;\widehat J)\le\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})$. Applying Fano [F8] and the finite mutual-information identity [F9], with $H(J)=\ln M$, yields $(1-e)\ln M\le\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})+\ln2$. For $M=1$, [F2] gives $\chi(\{1,\omega_1\})=S(\omega_1)-S(\omega_1)=0$, so the inequality is $0\le\ln2$.

Since $\eta_n\to0$, choose $N$ large enough that $p^{\otimes n}(T_n)=1-\eta_n>0$ and $\eta_n\le1/2$ for every $n\ge N$. For the finite prefix $n<N$, set $M_n=1$ and use the one-message code from step 1.2. For $n\ge N$, set $M_n=\lfloor e^{nR}\rfloor$ and apply the packing lemma [F5] to the conditional input law on $T_n$, with $d=e^{n(H(B|X)+\delta)}$ and $D^{-1}=(1-\eta_n)^{-1}e^{-n(S(\bar\rho_p)-\delta)}$. It gives expected average error at most $$2(u_n+2\sqrt{u_n})+4(M_n-1)(1-\eta_n)^{-1}e^{-n(\chi_p-2\delta)}.$$ Since $(1-\eta_n)^{-1}\le2$ for $n\ge N$ and $R<\chi_p-2\delta$, this tends to zero. The codebook space is finite; order $\mathcal X$ once and choose its lexicographically first codebook whose average error is at most this expectation. This defines a deterministic code for each $n\ge N$ without any choice axiom, and the finite one-message prefix does not affect $n^{-1}\ln M_n\to R$.

Let $p_i(x)=M^{-1}|\{m:x_i(m)=x\}|$ and $\bar\omega=M^{-1}\sum_m\omega_m$. By [F17], its $i$th marginal is $\bar\rho_i=\sum_xp_i(x)\rho_x$, which is a state by [F16]. For any bipartite state $\tau_{AC}$, tensor it with the unique state on a one-dimensional middle register $B=\mathbb C$: the four entropies in [F6] become $S(\tau_A),S(\tau_C),0,S(\tau_{AC})$, because tensoring with this factor leaves the spectrum unchanged. Thus [F6] implies $S(\tau_{AC})\le S(\tau_A)+S(\tau_C)$; iterating gives $S(\bar\omega)\le\sum_iS(\bar\rho_i)$. Product entropy is additive: diagonalize each $\rho_{x_i(m)}$ by [F12], so every positive product eigenvalue has logarithm equal to the sum of its coordinate logarithms by [F13]; zero eigenvalues contribute zero by [F2]. Summing these finite terms gives $S(\omega_m)=\sum_iS(\rho_{x_i(m)})$. Therefore $$\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})=S(\bar\omega)-\frac1M\sum_mS(\omega_m) \le\sum_{i=1}^n\left[S(\bar\rho_i)-\sum_xp_i(x)S(\rho_x)\right] =\sum_i\chi_{p_i}\le n\chi_*.$$

The selected codes have average error tending to zero and $n^{-1}\ln M_n\to R$. If $R=0$, the single-message code has zero error. When $\chi_*>0$, taking a maximizing $p$ from step 1.1 proves achievability of every $0\le R<\chi_*$. When $\chi_*=0$, the single-message code shows that rate zero is reliable.

Combining steps 1.3 and 2.2 gives $(1-e)\ln M\le n\chi_*+\ln2$. For any reliable sequence, divide by $n$ and let $n\to\infty$; since $e_n\to0$, its limiting upper rate is at most $\chi_*$. Together with step 3.1 and the capacity definition [F1], this proves the theorem.

Fix a finite-input cq channel as in [[def-it-classical-quantum-memoryless-channel]]. For integers $n,M\ge1$, an $(n,M)$ **cq block code** consists of a deterministic encoder $m\mapsto x^n(m)\in\mathcal X^n$ for $m\in[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ and a finite POVM ([[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]) $(\Lambda_m)_{m\in[M]}$ on $H_B^{\otimes n}$. Under a uniform message, its **average block error** is
$$e_n:=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\left(1-\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda_m\rho_{x^n(m)})\right).$$
Its rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$ nats per channel use, using the natural-log unit convention of [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]]. A sequence of such codes is reliable if $e_n\to0$. The **classical capacity** $C_{\rm cq}$ is the supremum of $\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n$ over reliable sequences.

For each transmitted state, the POVM outcome weights sum to one by [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]], so $e_n$ is the uniform-message block error probability.

All logarithms are natural. First, for every density operator $\rho$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional space and every $\delta>0$, there are spectral projectors $\Pi_n$ for $\rho^{\otimes n}$ such that, as $n\to\infty$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_n\rho^{\otimes n})\to1,\qquad \operatorname{rank}\Pi_n\le e^{n(S(\rho)+\delta)},\qquad \Pi_n\rho^{\otimes n}\Pi_n\preceq e^{-n(S(\rho)-\delta)}\Pi_n.$$

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points

Fix a finite-input cq channel as in [[def-it-classical-quantum-memoryless-channel]]. For integers $n,M\ge1$, an $(n,M)$ **cq block code** consists of a deterministic encoder $m\mapsto x^n(m)\in\mathcal X^n$ for $m\in[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ and a finite POVM ([[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]) $(\Lambda_m)_{m\in[M]}$ on $H_B^{\otimes n}$. Under a uniform message, its **average block error** is
$$e_n:=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\left(1-\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda_m\rho_{x^n(m)})\right).$$
Its rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$ nats per channel use, using the natural-log unit convention of [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]]. A sequence of such codes is reliable if $e_n\to0$. The **classical capacity** $C_{\rm cq}$ is the supremum of $\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n$ over reliable sequences.

For each transmitted state, the POVM outcome weights sum to one by [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]], so $e_n$ is the uniform-message block error probability.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty classical label set, represented by a register $H_X$ with computational orthonormal basis $(\xi_x)_{x\in X}$ ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). For each $x$, write $\Pi_xz:=\langle z,\xi_x\rangle\xi_x$, the rank-one orthogonal projection using the root linear-first convention, as in [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Let $H_B$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. A finite **classical-quantum state** is

$$\rho_{XB}:=\sum_{x\in X}p_x\Pi_x\otimes\rho_x,$$

where $p_x\ge0$, $\sum_xp_x=1$, and each $\rho_x$ is a density operator on $H_B$. It is a density operator by [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Its quantum marginal is $\bar\rho_B:=\sum_xp_x\rho_x=\operatorname{Tr}_X\rho_{XB}$ by the second-factor partial-trace formula in [[def-qc-partial-trace]], and it is a density operator by [[lem-it-partial-traces-of-a-state-are-states]]. The **Holevo information** of this ensemble is

$$\chi(\{p_x,\rho_x\}_{x\in X}):=S(\bar\rho_B)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x),$$

where zero-probability branches contribute nothing. This is measured in nats under [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]].

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $(p_x)$ be a probability vector, let $\rho_x$ be density operators on a nonzero finite-dimensional space $H_B$, and let $\bar\rho:=\sum_xp_x\rho_x$. For a finite POVM $(E_y)_{y\in Y}$ on $H_B$, define $w(y\mid x):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_xE_y)$, $q_y:=\sum_xp_xw(y\mid x)$, and the classical mutual information

$$I(X:Y):=\sum_{x,y:p_xw(y\mid x)>0}p_xw(y\mid x)\ln\frac{w(y\mid x)}{q_y}.$$

Then

$$I(X:Y)\le\chi(\{p_x,\rho_x\})=S(\bar\rho)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x).$$

All logarithms are natural. First, for every density operator $\rho$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional space and every $\delta>0$, there are spectral projectors $\Pi_n$ for $\rho^{\otimes n}$ such that, as $n\to\infty$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_n\rho^{\otimes n})\to1,\qquad \operatorname{rank}\Pi_n\le e^{n(S(\rho)+\delta)},\qquad \Pi_n\rho^{\otimes n}\Pi_n\preceq e^{-n(S(\rho)-\delta)}\Pi_n.$$

Second, let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ be a probability vector, and let $\sigma_x$ be density operators on a nonzero finite-dimensional output space. Put $\bar\sigma=\sum_xp_x\sigma_x$ and $H(B|X)=\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\sigma_x)$. $$\operatorname{tr}(\Pi_n\bar\sigma^{\otimes n})\to1,\quad \operatorname{tr}(\Pi_n\bigotimes_i\sigma_{x_i})\ge1-u_n,\quad \operatorname{tr}(\Pi_{x^n}\bigotimes_i\sigma_{x_i})\ge1-u_n,$$
$$\operatorname{rank}\Pi_n\le e^{n(S(\bar\sigma)+\delta)},\quad \Pi_n\bar\sigma^{\otimes n}\Pi_n\preceq e^{-n(S(\bar\sigma)-\delta)}\Pi_n,$$
$$\operatorname{rank}\Pi_{x^n}\le e^{n(H(B|X)+\delta)},\quad \Pi_{x^n}\left(\bigotimes_i\sigma_{x_i}\right)\Pi_{x^n}\preceq e^{-n(H(B|X)-\delta)}\Pi_{x^n}.$$
Zero eigenvalues are omitted from surprisal sums. No identical-distribution assumption is made for the conditional eigenbasis measurements.

$$H(X,Y|Z)=H(X|Z)+H(Y|X,Z),$$

and

$$I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z).$$

In particular, $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)$. All terms are finite.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

derivations.claim: Write $\chi_*=\sup_{p\in\Delta(\mathcal X)}\chi_p$. The simplex is nonempty, closed, and bounded. For each state $\rho_x$, [F12] diagonalizes it with nonnegative eigenvalues summing to one by [F16], so its action on a unit vector has norm at most one and [F15] gives $\|\rho_x\|\le1$. Therefore $\|\bar\rho_p-\bar\rho_q\|\le\sum_x|p_x-q_x|$. Fix an orthonormal basis identifying $H_B$ unitarily with $\mathbb C^{\dim H_B}$; this preserves spectra and operator norm, so [F7] applies. Thus the first entropy term in $\chi_p$ is continuous in $p$; the second is a finite linear sum. Thus [F14] shows the supremum is attained, so $\chi_*=\max_p\chi_p$. A point-mass input law gives $\chi_p=0$ by [F2], hence $\chi_*\ge0$.

Fix $p$ and $0<R<\chi_p$. Choose $\delta>0$ with $R<\chi_p-2\delta$. Let $T_n$ be the input typical set from [F4], with excluded probability $\eta_n\to0$. Since $\eta_n\to0$, $p^{\otimes n}(T_n)=1-\eta_n>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$; for each earlier blocklength choose a fixed $x_0\in\mathcal X$ and use the one-message code with word $x_0^n$ and decoding POVM $\{I\}$. Draw each large-$n$ codeword independently from $p^{\otimes n}$ conditioned on $T_n$. Its mean output state is $$\bar\sigma_n'=\mathbb E[\rho_{X^n}\mid X^n\in T_n]\preceq(1-\eta_n)^{-1}\bar\rho_p^{\otimes n},\qquad \bar\rho_p=\sum_xp_x\rho_x.$$ The global typical projector from [F4] therefore obeys $\Pi_n\bar\sigma_n'\Pi_n\preceq(1-\eta_n)^{-1}e^{-n(S(\bar\rho_p)-\delta)}\Pi_n$. Each conditional projector has acceptance at least $1-u_n$, rank at most $e^{n(H(B|X)+\delta)}$, and the global projector accepts every conditioned codeword with at least $1-u_n$, where $u_n\to0$ and $H(B|X)=\sum_xp_xS(\rho_x)$.

Consider any $(n,M)$ code with $M\ge2$, uniform message $J$, output states $\omega_m=\bigotimes_i\rho_{x_i(m)}$, decoding outcome $\widehat J$, and average error $e$. The Holevo measurement bound [F3] gives $I(J;\widehat J)\le\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})$. Applying Fano [F8] and the finite mutual-information identity [F9], with $H(J)=\ln M$, yields $(1-e)\ln M\le\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})+\ln2$. For $M=1$, [F2] gives $\chi(\{1,\omega_1\})=S(\omega_1)-S(\omega_1)=0$, so the inequality is $0\le\ln2$.

Since $\eta_n\to0$, choose $N$ large enough that $p^{\otimes n}(T_n)=1-\eta_n>0$ and $\eta_n\le1/2$ for every $n\ge N$. For the finite prefix $n<N$, set $M_n=1$ and use the one-message code from step 1.2. For $n\ge N$, set $M_n=\lfloor e^{nR}\rfloor$ and apply the packing lemma [F5] to the conditional input law on $T_n$, with $d=e^{n(H(B|X)+\delta)}$ and $D^{-1}=(1-\eta_n)^{-1}e^{-n(S(\bar\rho_p)-\delta)}$. It gives expected average error at most $$2(u_n+2\sqrt{u_n})+4(M_n-1)(1-\eta_n)^{-1}e^{-n(\chi_p-2\delta)}.$$ Since $(1-\eta_n)^{-1}\le2$ for $n\ge N$ and $R<\chi_p-2\delta$, this tends to zero. The packing POVM has a failure effect $\Lambda_0$. Replace it by the $M_n$ effects $\Lambda_1\prime=\Lambda_1+\Lambda_0$ and $\Lambda_m\prime=\Lambda_m$ for $2\le m\le M_n$. They are positive and sum to $I$. For message 1 the success probability increases by the nonnegative quantity $\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda_0\rho_{x^n(1)})$, and for other messages it is unchanged; hence the merged average error is no larger for every codebook and obeys the same expectation bound. The codebook space is finite; order $\mathcal X$ once and choose its lexicographically first codebook whose average error is at most this expectation. This defines a deterministic code for each $n\ge N$ without any choice axiom, and the finite one-message prefix does not affect $n^{-1}\ln M_n\to R$.

Let $p_i(x)=M^{-1}|\{m:x_i(m)=x\}|$ and $\bar\omega=M^{-1}\sum_m\omega_m$. By [F17], its $i$th marginal is $\bar\rho_i=\sum_xp_i(x)\rho_x$, which is a state by [F16]. For any bipartite state $\tau_{AC}$, tensor it with the unique state on a one-dimensional middle register $B=\mathbb C$: the four entropies in [F6] become $S(\tau_A),S(\tau_C),0,S(\tau_{AC})$, because tensoring with this factor leaves the spectrum unchanged. Thus [F6] implies $S(\tau_{AC})\le S(\tau_A)+S(\tau_C)$; iterating gives $S(\bar\omega)\le\sum_iS(\bar\rho_i)$. Product entropy is additive: diagonalize each $\rho_{x_i(m)}$ by [F12], so every positive product eigenvalue has logarithm equal to the sum of its coordinate logarithms by [F13]; zero eigenvalues contribute zero by [F2]. Summing these finite terms gives $S(\omega_m)=\sum_iS(\rho_{x_i(m)})$. Therefore $$\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})=S(\bar\omega)-\frac1M\sum_mS(\omega_m) \le\sum_{i=1}^n\left[S(\bar\rho_i)-\sum_xp_i(x)S(\rho_x)\right] =\sum_i\chi_{p_i}\le n\chi_*.$$

The selected codes have average error tending to zero and $n^{-1}\ln M_n\to R$. If $R=0$, the single-message code has zero error. When $\chi_*>0$, taking a maximizing $p$ from step 1.1 proves achievability of every $0\le R<\chi_*$. When $\chi_*=0$, the single-message code shows that rate zero is reliable.

Combining steps 1.3 and 2.2 gives $(1-e)\ln M\le n\chi_*+\ln2$. For any reliable sequence, divide by $n$ and let $n\to\infty$; since $e_n\to0$, its limiting upper rate is at most $\chi_*$. Together with step 3.1 and the capacity definition [F1], this proves the theorem.

Fix a finite-input cq channel as in [[def-it-classical-quantum-memoryless-channel]]. For integers $n,M\ge1$, an $(n,M)$ **cq block code** consists of a deterministic encoder $m\mapsto x^n(m)\in\mathcal X^n$ for $m\in[M]:=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ and a finite POVM ([[def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law]]) $(\Lambda_m)_{m\in[M]}$ on $H_B^{\otimes n}$. Under a uniform message, its **average block error** is
$$e_n:=\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\left(1-\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda_m\rho_{x^n(m)})\right).$$
Its rate is $n^{-1}\ln M$ nats per channel use, using the natural-log unit convention of [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]]. A sequence of such codes is reliable if $e_n\to0$. The **classical capacity** $C_{\rm cq}$ is the supremum of $\liminf_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\ln M_n$ over reliable sequences.

For each transmitted state, the POVM outcome weights sum to one by [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]], so $e_n$ is the uniform-message block error probability.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty input alphabet and let $H_B$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. A **finite-input cq channel** is a map $x\mapsto\rho_x$ assigning a density operator ([[def-qc-density-operator]]) $\rho_x$ on $H_B$ to each $x\in\mathcal X$. Its $n$-use memoryless extension sends a word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ to the product state
$$\rho_{x^n}:=\rho_{x_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_{x_n}\quad\text{on }H_B^{\otimes n}.$$
For an input probability vector $p$, write $\bar\rho_p=\sum_xp_x\rho_x$ and $\chi_p=S(\bar\rho_p)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x)$; this is the Holevo information of the ensemble in [[def-it-classical-quantum-state-and-holevo-information]], in nats.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty classical label set, represented by a register $H_X$ with computational orthonormal basis $(\xi_x)_{x\in X}$ ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). For each $x$, write $\Pi_xz:=\langle z,\xi_x\rangle\xi_x$, the rank-one orthogonal projection using the root linear-first convention, as in [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Let $H_B$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. A finite **classical-quantum state** is

$$\rho_{XB}:=\sum_{x\in X}p_x\Pi_x\otimes\rho_x,$$

where $p_x\ge0$, $\sum_xp_x=1$, and each $\rho_x$ is a density operator on $H_B$. It is a density operator by [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Its quantum marginal is $\bar\rho_B:=\sum_xp_x\rho_x=\operatorname{Tr}_X\rho_{XB}$ by the second-factor partial-trace formula in [[def-qc-partial-trace]], and it is a density operator by [[lem-it-partial-traces-of-a-state-are-states]]. The **Holevo information** of this ensemble is

$$\chi(\{p_x,\rho_x\}_{x\in X}):=S(\bar\rho_B)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x),$$

where zero-probability branches contribute nothing. This is measured in nats under [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]].

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $(p_x)$ be a probability vector, let $\rho_x$ be density operators on a nonzero finite-dimensional space $H_B$, and let $\bar\rho:=\sum_xp_x\rho_x$. For a finite POVM $(E_y)_{y\in Y}$ on $H_B$, define $w(y\mid x):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_xE_y)$, $q_y:=\sum_xp_xw(y\mid x)$, and the classical mutual information

$$I(X:Y):=\sum_{x,y:p_xw(y\mid x)>0}p_xw(y\mid x)\ln\frac{w(y\mid x)}{q_y}.$$

$$I(X:Y)\le\chi(\{p_x,\rho_x\})=S(\bar\rho)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x).$$

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

finite_smoke.asserts: 1.3 Consider any $(n,M)$ code with $M\ge2$, uniform message $J$, output states $\omega_m=\bigotimes_i\rho_{x_i(m)}$, decoding outcome $\widehat J$, and average error $e$. The Holevo measurement bound [F3] gives $I(J;\widehat J)\le\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})$. Applying Fano [F8] and the finite mutual-information identity [F9], with $H(J)=\ln M$, yields $(1-e)\ln M\le\chi(\{1/M,\omega_m\})+\ln2$. For $M=1$, [F2] gives $\chi(\{1,\omega_1\})=S(\omega_1)-S(\omega_1)=0$, so the inequality is $0\le\ln2$. [F1, F2, F3, F8, F9, given, algebra, cases]
